{{Short description|Mathematical function related to dynamical systems}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''Parry–Daniels map''' is a [[function (mathematics)|function]] studied in the context of [[dynamical systems]]. Typical questions concern the existence of an [[invariant measure|invariant]] or [[ergodic (adjective)|ergodic measure]] for the map.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zweimüller |first=Roland |title=Surrey Notes on Infinite Ergodic Theory |url=https://mat.univie.ac.at/~zweimueller/MyPub/SurreyNotes.pdf}}</ref>

It is named after the [[England|English]] [[mathematician]] [[Bill Parry (mathematician)|Bill Parry]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Parry |first=William |date=1962 |title=Ergodic Properties of Some Permutation Processes |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2333475 |journal=Biometrika |volume=49 |issue=1/2 |pages=151–154 |doi=10.2307/2333475 |jstor=2333475 |issn=0006-3444|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and the [[UK|British]] [[statistician]] [[Henry Daniels (statistician)|Henry Daniels]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Daniels |first=H. E. |date=1962 |title=Processes Generating Permutation Expansions |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2333474 |journal=Biometrika |volume=49 |issue=1/2 |pages=139–149 |doi=10.2307/2333474 |jstor=2333474 |issn=0006-3444|url-access=subscription }}</ref> who independently studied the map in papers published in 1962.

==Definition==
Given an [[integer]] ''n''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;1, let Σ denote the ''n''-[[dimension]]al [[simplex]] in '''R'''<sup>''n''+1</sup> given by

:<math>\Sigma := \{ x = (x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^{n + 1} | 0 \leq x_i \leq 1 \mbox{ for each } i \mbox{ and } x_0 + x_1 + \dots + x_n = 1 \}.</math>

Let ''&pi;'' be a [[permutation]] such that

:<math>x_{\pi(0)} \leq x_{\pi (1)} \leq \dots \leq x_{\pi (n)}.</math>

Then the '''Parry–Daniels map'''

: <math>T_{\pi} : \Sigma \to \Sigma</math>

is defined by

:<math>T_\pi (x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n) := \left( \frac{x_{\pi (0)}}{x_{\pi (n)}} , \frac{x_{\pi (1)} - x_{\pi (0)}}{x_{\pi (n)}}, \dots, \frac{x_{\pi (n)} - x_{\pi (n - 1)}}{x_{\pi (n)}} \right).</math>
